title: First words
goal: Greet people politely in both Kolkata and Dhaka styles, say yes/no, please, thank you and sorry, and choose the right word for 'you'.
intro:
Bengali greetings follow community lines more than borders. **নমস্কার** *nômoshkar* (palms together) is used among Hindus and in formal West Bengal settings; **আসসালামু আলাইকুম** *assalamu alaikum* is the everyday greeting among Muslims and in most of Bangladesh. If in doubt, a smile and **কেমন আছেন?** *kæmon achhen?* ('How are you?') works with everyone.

The most important choice you make in every sentence is **which 'you'** to use. Start with respectful **আপনি** *apni* for everyone you don't know well.

vocab.note: Said with palms joined. Informal: নমস্তে is rarely used in Bengali.

vocab.en: and peace be on you (reply to assalamu alaikum)

vocab.note: Nasal æ, like a nasal 'ha' in 'hat'.
Also negates verbs, placed after them: যাই না 'I don't go'.
Used less than in English; among friends a smile is enough. Many Bangladeshis also say থ্যাংক ইউ.
Quite formal; politeness is normally shown with the verb form and একটু.
আমি দুঃখিত 'I am sorry'. Colloquially: সরি.
To a friend: মাফ করো (maf kôro). WB also ক্ষমা করবেন (khôma kôrben).
A translation of the English greeting; used in writing and formal settings more than in daily speech.
Rather solemn; everyday goodbyes are আসি or আবার দেখা হবে.
Bengalis avoid saying 'I'm going' (যাই) when leaving; আসি 'I'll come (back)' is preferred. Reply: এসো / আসুন.
Friends, colleagues your age, younger people, family members in many homes.
Close friends, siblings, small children. Rude to strangers!
Spelled কি; the word 'what' is spelled কী. Both are pronounced ki.
Adding একটু makes a request polite: একটু বসুন 'please sit'.

phrases.en: Take care. (polite; to a friend: ভালো থেকো)

grammar.title: Word order: subject – object – verb
grammar.body:
Bengali puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence. The usual order is **Subject – (time/place) – Object – Verb**. 'I speak Bengali' is literally *I Bengali speak*: আমি বাংলা বলি.

Negation is easy: in the present tense **না** comes **after** the verb: আমি বলি না 'I don't speak'. Yes/no questions keep the same order and simply add **কি** after the subject (or rely on intonation).

In the present tense Bengali usually has **no word for 'is/am/are'** with adjectives and nouns: আমি ভালো 'I (am) good'. But for *being somewhere* or *being in a state* (like 'How are you?') it uses **আছ-** 'to be present': আমি ভালো আছি 'I am well'.

grammar.title: Three kinds of 'you': আপনি, তুমি, তুই
grammar.body:
Bengali has three second-person pronouns, and **the verb changes with each**:

**আপনি** *apni* – respectful: strangers, elders, teachers, shopkeepers. Verb ending **-েন** (*-en*): আপনি আছেন, আপনি বলেন.
**তুমি** *tumi* – familiar: friends, peers, younger people, and in many families, parents. Verb ending **-ো** (*-o*): তুমি আছো, তুমি বলো.
**তুই** *tui* – intimate: best friends, siblings, small children. Verb ending **-িস** (*-ish*): তুই আছিস, তুই বলিস.

Using তুই with a stranger is insulting; using আপনি with a close friend sounds cold. Learners should default to **আপনি**; people will invite you to switch (তুমি করে বলো 'say tumi').

examples.en: Call me tumi (you can be informal with me).

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Sara, a student from abroad, meets her elderly neighbour Mr Rahman on the stairs in Dhaka.

lines.speaker: Mr Rahman
lines.en: Hello. How are you, dear? (lit. 'mother', affectionate)

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.native: ভালো আছি, ধন্যবাদ। আপনি কেমন আছেন?
lines.roman: bhalo achhi, dhônnobad. apni kæmon achhen?
lines.en: I'm fine, thanks. How are you?

lines.speaker: Mr Rahman
lines.native: এই তো, চলছে। তুমি বাংলা বলো?
lines.roman: ei to, cholchhe. tumi baṅla bôlo?

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.native: মাফ করবেন, আমি এখন একটু ব্যস্ত। আসি?
lines.roman: maf kôrben, ami ækhon ekṭu bæsto. ashi?
lines.en: Excuse me, I'm a bit busy now. May I go? (lit. 'shall I come?')

culture: Older people often address younger women as মা (*ma*, 'mother') and younger men as বাবা (*baba*, 'father') as a term of affection. Elders are never called by their first name: use relationship words like দাদা/ভাই (elder brother), দিদি/আপা (elder sister), কাকু/চাচা (uncle) even for strangers. In West Bengal a Hindu would answer নমস্কার with নমস্কার; in Bangladesh most people greet with সালাম. Saying যাই 'I'm going' when leaving can sound ominous; say আসি 'I'll come (again)'.
